entries.claim: FID fits a Gaussian (mean and covariance) to Inception-v3 coding-layer features of real and of generated images and takes the Frechet (Wasserstein-2) distance between the two Gaussians.
entries.quote: We call the Fréchet distance d(., .) between the Gaussian with mean (m, C) obtained from p(.) and the Gaussian with mean (mw , Cw ) obtained from pw (.) the "Fréchet Inception Distance" (FID), which is given by: d^2((m, C), (mw, Cw)) = ||m - mw||_2^2 + Tr(C + Cw - 2(C Cw)^(1/2))
entries.source: Heusel et al. 2017, GANs Trained by a Two Time-Scale Update Rule Converge to a Local Nash Equilibrium
entries.where: Section 'Experiments', Eq. (6) (arXiv PDF v6; no arXiv HTML version exists, ar5iv conversion failed)
entries.note: Formula re-typed from PDF text extraction. The paper says 'For practical reasons we only consider the first two polynomials, that is, the first two moments: mean and covariance.'

entries.claim: The paper uses the last pooling layer of Inception-v3 as the coding layer, real statistics from the whole training set, and 50,000 generated images.
entries.quote: For computing the FID, we propagated all images from the training dataset through the pretrained Inception-v3 model following the computation of the Inception Score [53], however, we use the last pooling layer as coding layer. ... To approximate these moments for the model distribution, we generate 50,000 images
entries.source: Heusel et al. 2017, GANs Trained by a Two Time-Scale Update Rule Converge to a Local Nash Equilibrium
entries.note: The 2048 dimension is not stated in the paper text; it is stated in the official TTUR README (see fid_min_sample_size).

entries.claim: The official FID code README recommends at least 10,000 samples, says the sample count must exceed the 2048 feature dimension, and warns that too few samples underestimate the true FID.
entries.quote: The number of samples to calculate the Gaussian statistics (mean and covariance) should be greater than the dimension of the coding layer, here 2048 for the Inception pool 3 layer. Otherwise the covariance is not full rank resulting in complex numbers and nans by calculating the square root. We recommend using a minimum sample size of 10,000 to calculate the FID otherwise the true FID of the generator is underestimated.
entries.source: Heusel et al., official TTUR / FID code README (bioinf-jku/TTUR)
entries.where: README.md lines 15--21, master at commit ec6561000644ef798b4a358846b1aee481332045
entries.note: The recommendation is in the code README, not in the paper. 'underestimated' is the README's word; Chong and Forsyth show the finite-N bias is positive (FID_N is larger than FID_infinity), so read 'underestimated' as 'quality underestimated' or treat the wording with care.

entries.claim: FID computed with N samples is biased, and the bias depends on the generator, so fixing N does not make comparisons fair.
entries.quote: the paper shows that the bias term depends on the particular model being evaluated, so model A may get a better score than model B simply because model A's bias term is smaller. This effect cannot be fixed by evaluating at a fixed number of samples.
entries.source: Chong and Forsyth 2020, Effectively Unbiased FID and Inception Score and where to find them

entries.claim: Expected FID_N equals the true FID plus a term K/N (K depends on the generator) plus O(1/N^2), so FID is linear in 1/N and can be extrapolated to N to infinity.
entries.quote: FID is linear with respect to 1/N and different generators have very different K, so that generators cannot be compared with FID_N for any finite N (section 4.1).
entries.source: Chong and Forsyth 2020, Effectively Unbiased FID and Inception Score and where to find them
entries.where: Section 3.1 (E[G(I_hat)] = G(I) + K/N + O(1/N^2)) and Section 4 summary list
entries.note: FID_infinity bar is obtained by fitting a line to FID_N vs 1/N and reading the intercept; they also use Sobol (quasi Monte Carlo) latent samples to reduce variance.

entries.claim: The bias vanishes as N grows and the O(1/N^2) terms are small, so extrapolating a line in 1/N gives an effectively unbiased FID_infinity.
entries.quote: The bias in FID_N vanishes for N→∞. Figure 2 suggests that the O(1/N^2) terms are small for practical N, so we can extrapolate in 1/N to obtain FID_infinity bar (an estimate of the value of FID_infinity).
entries.source: Chong and Forsyth 2020, Effectively Unbiased FID and Inception Score and where to find them

entries.claim: Two independently trained DCGANs with identical architecture swap order depending on the N used for FID.
entries.quote: The graph compares the FID_N vs 1/N between two independently trained identical architecture DCGANs. At marker 1, DCGAN 1 is better than DCGAN 2; at marker 2 they are approximately the same; at marker 3 DCGAN 2 is better than DCGAN 1. This shows that comparisons between models of a fixed N are unreliable.
entries.source: Chong and Forsyth 2020, Effectively Unbiased FID and Inception Score and where to find them
entries.note: The figure is a plot; the exact FID values at the markers are not given in text.

entries.claim: Papers differ in N: some report FID at 50k samples, others at 10k.
entries.quote: Evaluation procedures with FID vary: some authors use FID_50k [7, 19, 18] while others use FID_10k [37, 25].
entries.source: Chong and Forsyth 2020, Effectively Unbiased FID and Inception Score and where to find them

entries.claim: Common FID code (PyTorch-FID, TensorFlow-FID) resizes to 299x299 with a fixed-width bilinear filter that aliases; PIL's filters widen with the downsampling factor and antialias, so clean-fid proposes PIL bicubic.
entries.quote: The FID implementations in PyTorch and TensorFlow use a fixed-width bilinear interpolation, independent of resizing ratio. In contrast, the proposed Clean-FID uses an implementation that follows standard signal processing principles and adaptively stretches the filter to prevent aliasing.
entries.source: Parmar, Zhang, Zhu 2022, On Aliased Resizing and Surprising Subtleties in GAN Evaluation (CVPR 2022)
entries.where: Figure 2 caption; Section 1 ('we propose to use a stronger bicubic filter')

entries.claim: The same 1024px FFHQ real images resized to 299 with different libraries already differ by FID 0.64 (PIL bilinear), 4.34 (TensorFlow bilinear), 4.36 (PyTorch bilinear) and 7.43 (naive nearest) versus PIL bicubic.
entries.quote: Table 1 left (PIL-bicubic(Real) vs Resize(Real)), FID / KIDx10^3 / PSNR: PIL-bilinear 0.64 / 0.61 / 45.7; TensorFlow-bilinear 4.34 / 4.32 / 37.66; PyTorch-bilinear 4.36 / 4.31 / 37.66; Naive nearest 7.43 / 7.54 / 35.16
entries.source: Parmar, Zhang, Zhu 2022, On Aliased Resizing and Surprising Subtleties in GAN Evaluation
entries.note: Text rounds these as 'FID 4.3' and 'FID 7.4'; consistent with the table.

entries.claim: For StyleGAN2 FFHQ samples scored against PIL-bicubic reference statistics, using a different resizer for the generated images moves FID from 2.98 to 4.03 (PIL bilinear), 7.45 (TF or PyTorch bilinear) and 10.67 (naive nearest).
entries.quote: Table 1 right (PIL-bicubic(Real) vs Resize(StyleGAN2)), FID / KIDx10^3: PIL-bicubic 2.98 / 0.51; PIL-bilinear 4.03 / 1.52; TensorFlow-bilinear 7.45 / 5.12; PyTorch-bilinear 7.45 / 5.15; Naive nearest 10.67 / 8.47
entries.source: Parmar, Zhang, Zhu 2022, On Aliased Resizing and Surprising Subtleties in GAN Evaluation

entries.claim: When the same resizer is used for both sets, aliased resizers give lower (better looking) FIDs, e.g. MetFaces 65.32 with PIL bicubic vs 57.46 with PyTorch bilinear.
entries.quote: Table 2, FID (FFHQ / MetFaces / AFHQ-Cats / AFHQ-Dogs): PIL-bicubic 2.98 / 65.32 / 5.13 / 20.16; PIL-bilinear 2.99 / 64.31 / 5.01 / 19.60; TensorFlow-bilinear 2.75 / 57.45 / 4.93 / 19.45; PyTorch-bilinear 2.75 / 57.46 / 4.94 / 19.46; Naive nearest 2.68 / 55.09 / 4.80 / 18.25. Caption: 'Interestingly, the downsampling methods that alias result in lower scores'
entries.source: Parmar, Zhang, Zhu 2022, On Aliased Resizing and Surprising Subtleties in GAN Evaluation

entries.claim: Resizing the FFHQ training set (1024 to 256) with different functions before training StyleGAN2 changes the final FID from 4.82 (naive nearest) to 6.21 (PIL bicubic), mean of three runs.
entries.quote: Table 3, FID on FFHQ: Naive Nearest 4.82 ± 0.09; PyTorch-bilinear 5.13 ± 0.20; TensorFlow-bilinear 5.08 ± 0.16; PIL-bicubic 6.21 ± 0.23
entries.source: Parmar, Zhang, Zhu 2022, On Aliased Resizing and Surprising Subtleties in GAN Evaluation

entries.claim: Saving real FFHQ 256px images as JPEG at the PIL default quality 75 gives FID about 21 against the PNG originals, far above StyleGAN2's FID of about 3, although the images look identical.
entries.quote: Despite being perceptually indistinguishable (with high PSNR values of ≥ 39), the FID scores increase. The PIL default of 75 results in a high score (21), for example. Note that this FID score is far higher than the score from a powerful generative model, StyleGAN2 [38] (around 3). Also, variations across recent methods are typically within 1 FID on FFHQ.
entries.source: Parmar, Zhang, Zhu 2022, On Aliased Resizing and Surprising Subtleties in GAN Evaluation

entries.claim: On LSUN Church (collected as JPEG-75), compressing StyleGAN2's generated images with JPEG quality 87 improves FID from 4.00 (PNG) to 3.48.
entries.quote: we show that if compression is used on real training images, FID can actually improve if the generated images are also subsequently compressed. ... the best FID score (3.48) is obtained when the generated images are compressed with JPEG quality 87 (not the full 75) ... The FID score for the generated images stores as PNG files is 4.00.
entries.source: Parmar, Zhang, Zhu 2022, On Aliased Resizing and Surprising Subtleties in GAN Evaluation
entries.where: Abstract/intro paragraph; Section 4.3 'JPEG on training images'; Figure 8 caption (4.00 → 3.48)
entries.note: Context: LSUN outdoor Church was stored as JPEG-75 at collection. For FFHQ (collected as PNG), 'Any additional compression only monotonically increases the FID score (Figure 8 right).' Text, Figure 8 caption and README all agree on 4.00 and 3.48.

entries.claim: The clean-fid library has mode='clean' (antialiased PIL resize) plus two backward-compatibility modes that reproduce pytorch-fid and the original TensorFlow TTUR code.
entries.quote: We provide two flags to reproduce the legacy FID score. - mode="legacy_pytorch" This flag is equivalent to using the popular PyTorch FID implementation ... The difference ... is ~2e-06 - mode="legacy_tensorflow" This flag is equivalent to using the official implementation of FID released by the authors. ... The difference ... is ~2e-05
entries.source: Parmar et al., clean-fid GitHub README (GaParmar/clean-fid)
entries.where: README 'Backwards Compatibility' section, lines 205--223, main at commit e88c4d6269a4bbf04c04deeb578475b57719acee
entries.note: README also offers model_name="clip_vit_b_32" to compute FID on CLIP features, citing Kynkaanniemi et al. 2022.

entries.claim: KID is the squared MMD between Inception representations of real and generated images with the cubic polynomial kernel k(x,y) = (x.y/d + 1)^3, d the feature dimension.
entries.quote: We propose a metric similar to the FID, the Kernel Inception Distance, to be the squared MMD between Inception representations. We use a polynomial kernel, k(x,y)=((1/d) x^T y+1)^3 where d is the representation dimension, to avoid correlations with the objective of MMD GANs as well as to avoid tuning any kernel parameters.
entries.source: Binkowski, Sutherland, Arbel, Gretton 2018, Demystifying MMD GANs
entries.note: Footnote 11: 'k is the default polynomial kernel in scikit-learn'. The paper also states FID uses 'the pool3 layer, of dimension 2048'.

entries.claim: Unlike FID, KID makes no Gaussian assumption, compares skewness as well as mean and variance, and has a simple unbiased estimator.
entries.quote: First, it does not assume a parametric form for the distribution of activations. This is particularly sensible since the representations have ReLU activations, and therefore are not only never negative, but do not even have a density: about 2% of components in Inception representations are typically exactly zero. With the cubic kernel we use here, the KID compares skewness as well as the mean and variance. Also, unlike the FID, the KID has a simple unbiased estimator.
entries.source: Binkowski et al. 2018, Demystifying MMD GANs

entries.claim: On CIFAR-10 train vs test (same distribution), KID is essentially 0 already at n = 2,000, while FID is still about 8.1 at n = 10,000 and still falling.
entries.quote: at n=2 000, when the KID estimator is essentially always 0, the FID estimator is still quite large. Even at n=10 000, the full size of the CIFAR test set, the FID still seems to be decreasing from its estimate of about 8.1 towards zero, showing the strong persistence of bias. This highlights that FID scores can only be compared to one another with the same value of n.
entries.source: Binkowski et al. 2018, Demystifying MMD GANs
entries.note: Footnote 10: 'in fact no unbiased estimator of the FID exists; see Section D.3.' Footnote 12 recommends small n averaged over several estimates (block estimator).

entries.claim: torch-fidelity v0.4.0 computes KID by default on 100 random subsets of 1,000 samples each with the poly kernel, degree 3, gamma None (becomes 1/d) and coef0 1.
entries.quote: "kid_subsets": 100, "kid_subset_size": 1000, "kid_kernel": "poly", "kid_kernel_poly_degree": 3, "kid_kernel_poly_gamma": None, "kid_kernel_poly_coef0": 1, "kid_kernel_rbf_sigma": 10,
entries.source: Obukhov et al., torch-fidelity v0.4.0 (toshas/torch-fidelity), torch_fidelity/defaults.py

entries.claim: In torch-fidelity v0.4.0, gamma None becomes 1/feature_dim, matching the paper's kernel, and the default MMD estimate drops the diagonal of K_XX and K_YY (unbiased); the reported KID is the mean (and std) over subsets.
entries.quote: if gamma is None: gamma = 1.0 / X.shape[1]; K = (np.matmul(X, Y.T) * gamma + coef0) ** degree ... def mmd2(K_XX, K_XY, K_YY, unit_diagonal=False, mmd_est="unbiased"): ... mmd2 = (Kt_XX_sum + Kt_YY_sum) / (m * (m - 1)); if mmd_est == "unbiased": mmd2 -= 2 * K_XY_sum / (m * m)
entries.source: Obukhov et al., torch-fidelity v0.4.0, torch_fidelity/metric_kid.py
entries.where: metric_kid.py lines 21 (mmd2 signature), 41--57 (estimator), 63--69 (kernel_poly), 116--128 (subset loop, KID mean)
entries.note: Subsets are drawn with rng.choice(..., replace=False) within a subset (lines 122--123).

entries.claim: Improved precision and recall estimate each manifold as the union of hyperspheres around every feature vector with radius equal to the distance to its k-th nearest neighbour; precision is the share of generated samples inside the real manifold, recall the share of real samples inside the generated manifold.
entries.quote: for each feature vector, forming a hypersphere with radius equal to the distance to its k th nearest neighbor. Together, these hyperspheres define a volume in the feature space that serves as an estimate of the true manifold. ... precision is quantified by querying for each generated image whether the image is within the estimated manifold of real images. Symmetrically, recall is calculated by querying for each real image whether the image is within estimated manifold of generated images.
entries.source: Kynkaanniemi, Karras, Laine, Lehtinen, Aila 2019, Improved Precision and Recall Metric for Assessing Generative Models

entries.claim: Features are VGG-16 activations after the second fully connected layer (fc2); they use k = 3 and 50,000 images per set.
entries.quote: we compute the feature vector φ for a given image by feeding it to a pre-trained VGG-16 classifier [28] and extracting the corresponding activation vector after the second fully connected layer. ... Tests with various datasets and GANs showed that k=3 is a robust choice that avoids saturating the values most of the time. Thus we use k=3 and |Φ|=50000 in all our experiments unless stated otherwise.
entries.source: Kynkaanniemi et al. 2019, Improved Precision and Recall Metric for Assessing Generative Models
entries.note: They report Inception-v3 features give 'very similar results' (Figure 3c).

entries.claim: Sajjadi et al. introduced precision and recall for distributions (PRD) to split the single FID-style number into quality and coverage.
entries.quote: these metrics are unable to distinguish between different failure cases since they only yield one-dimensional scores. We propose a novel definition of precision and recall for distributions which disentangles the divergence into two separate dimensions.
entries.source: Sajjadi, Bachem, Lucic, Bousquet, Gelly 2018, Assessing Generative Models via Precision and Recall

entries.claim: Density and coverage fix k-NN precision and recall's sensitivity to outliers: a single real outlier inflates the real manifold so fakes clustered near it raise precision; density counts how many real spheres contain each fake, coverage builds spheres around real samples only.
entries.quote: Because of the real outlier sample, the manifold is overestimated. Generating many fake samples around the real outlier is enough to increase the precision measure. ... the problem of overestimating precision (100%) in Figure 1a is resolved using the density measure (60%).
entries.source: Naeem, Oh, Uh, Choi, Yoo 2020, Reliable Fidelity and Diversity Metrics for Generative Models (ICML 2020)
entries.note: Abstract: P&R 'fail to detect the match between two identical distributions, they are not robust against outliers, and the evaluation hyperparameters are selected arbitrarily.' Density is not bounded by 1.

entries.claim: Resampling generated images so their Inception top-1 ImageNet class histogram matches the real data lowers FID by about 10% without visibly changing quality; non-ImageNet feature spaces (SwAV, CLIP) barely move.
entries.quote: Over multiple datasets, this simple Top-1 histogram matching consistently improves FID, by ∼10% (Table 1). Table 1, FFHQ: FID 5.30 → FID^Top-1 4.70 (-11.3%); FID_CLIP 2.76 → 2.74 (-0.7%). LSUN Cat: 8.25 → 7.37 (-10.7%); FID_CLIP 8.94 → 8.83 (-1.2%).
entries.source: Kynkaanniemi, Karras, Aittala, Aila, Lehtinen 2023, The Role of ImageNet Classes in Frechet Inception Distance (ICLR 2023)
entries.where: Section 3, 'Top-1 histogram matching', Table 1 (averages over five FID evaluations)

entries.claim: Resampling generated images to match all 'fringe' Inception features cuts FFHQ FID from 5.30 to 1.78 (-66.4%) while FID in CLIP space only drops 2.76 to 2.64 (-4.3%); the image grids show no obvious improvement.
entries.quote: Table 2 shows that FIDs can be drastically reduced using this approach. An improvement by as much as 60% would be considered a major breakthrough in generative modeling, and it should be completely obvious when looking at the generated images. Yet, the uncurated grids in Appendix D fail to demonstrate an indisputable improvement.
entries.source: Kynkaanniemi et al. 2023, The Role of ImageNet Classes in Frechet Inception Distance
entries.where: Section 3, 'Matching all fringe features', Table 2 (averages over ten FID evaluations)
entries.note: Text says 'as much as 60%'; Table 2 shows -66.4% (FFHQ), -63.0% (LSUN Cat), -62.7% (LSUN Car). Not a contradiction, the text rounds down.

entries.claim: A Projected FastGAN whose discriminator uses ImageNet-pretrained features gets FID comparable to StyleGAN2 on FFHQ but looks worse; FID in CLIP space agrees with the humans.
entries.quote: In this iso-FID comparison, FID_CLIP agrees with human assessment – StyleGAN2 is rated significantly better than Projected FastGAN. It therefore seems clear that Projected FastGAN has lower FID than it should have ... This observation does not mean that ImageNet pre-training is a bad idea, but it does mean that such pre-training can make FID unreliable in practice.
entries.source: Kynkaanniemi et al. 2023, The Role of ImageNet Classes in Frechet Inception Distance

entries.claim: In the largest human study of generative-model realism to date, no existing metric strongly correlated with human judgments, and diffusion models fooled humans more yet were ranked worse than GANs by FID.
entries.quote: we measure human perception of image realism for generated samples by conducting the largest experiment evaluating generative models to date, and find that no existing metric strongly correlates with human evaluations. Comparing to 17 modern metrics ... we find that the state-of-the-art perceptual realism of diffusion models as judged by humans is not reflected in commonly reported metrics such as FID. This discrepancy is not explained by diversity in generated samples, though one cause is over-reliance on Inception-V3.
entries.source: Stein et al. 2023, Exposing flaws of generative model evaluation metrics and their unfair treatment of diffusion models (NeurIPS 2023)
entries.note: Human metric is 'human error rate', the fraction of images incorrectly classified in a real-vs-fake test (40 practice trials then 200 test trials per participant, half real; Appendix C). Per-encoder correlation values are shown only in Figure 4 (plot), so no numeric r is recorded here.

entries.claim: Outside CIFAR-10, no common metric computed in Inception space correlates strongly with human error rate; swapping Inception for DINOv2-ViT-L/14 recovers the correlation.
entries.quote: We find no strong correlation between human evaluation and any common metric computed in the Inception representation space outside of the simplistic CIFAR10 dataset ... We have found that FID does not correlate with human error rate, and have shown that replacing the Inception-V3 network with an SSL encoder such as DINOv2-ViT-L/14 both recovers the correlation of FD with human error rate, and results in a metric which qualitatively focuses on the more relevant parts of images.
entries.source: Stein et al. 2023, Exposing flaws of generative model evaluation metrics and their unfair treatment of diffusion models
entries.where: Section 4 (after Figure 4) and start of Section 5
entries.note: 'Strong' is defined in the Figure 4 caption as |r| >= 0.5 with p <= 0.05 (Pearson).

entries.claim: The recommended encoder is DINOv2 ViT-L/14 (trained on 142M images); for all ViT encoders they use ViT-L/14 as a quality/compute trade-off, and they advocate replacing Inception-V3 entirely.
entries.quote: DINOv2 is a ViT-L/14 architecture trained on a large custom dataset of 142M images ... we advocate for a complete replacement of Inception-V3 in all evaluation metrics of images
entries.source: Stein et al. 2023, Exposing flaws of generative model evaluation metrics and their unfair treatment of diffusion models
entries.note: Code: github.com/layer6ai-labs/dgm-eval (cited by EDM2 as the implementation used).

entries.claim: EDM2-XXL reaches FID 1.91 without guidance and 1.81 with classifier-free guidance on ImageNet-512 (63 NFE).
entries.quote: Table 2, ImageNet-512, FID no CFG / w/CFG: EDM2-XS 3.53 / 2.91; EDM2-S 2.56 / 2.23; EDM2-M 2.25 / 2.01; EDM2-L 2.06 / 1.88; EDM2-XL 1.96 / 1.85; EDM2-XXL 1.91 / 1.81. Caption: 'The "w/CFG" and "no CFG" columns show the lowest FID obtained with and without classifier-free guidance'
entries.source: Karras et al. 2024, Analyzing and Improving the Training Dynamics of Diffusion Models (EDM2, CVPR 2024)
entries.where: Table 2 (arXiv PDF; arXiv HTML and ar5iv unavailable for this paper)
entries.note: Same table lists ADM 23.24/7.72, DiT-XL/2 12.03/3.04, VDM++ 2.99/2.65, StyleGAN-XL -/2.41.

entries.claim: In DINOv2 space EDM2-XXL scores FD_DINOv2 42.84 without guidance and 33.09 with guidance on ImageNet-512, computed with 50,000 generated images against all 1,281,167 ImageNet training images.
entries.quote: Table 5, FD_DINOv2 no CFG / w/CFG: EDM2-XS 103.39 / 79.94; EDM2-S 68.64 / 52.32; EDM2-M 58.44 / 41.98; EDM2-L 52.25 / 38.20; EDM2-XL 45.96 / 35.67; EDM2-XXL 42.84 / 33.09. Text: 'We use 50,000 generated images and all 1,281,167 available real images, following the established best practices in FID computation.'
entries.source: Karras et al. 2024, Analyzing and Improving the Training Dynamics of Diffusion Models (EDM2)
entries.note: FD_DINOv2 values are on a different scale from FID (tens, not ones). Table 5 caption copies Table 2's wording ('lowest FID') though the column is FD_DINOv2.

entries.claim: EDM2 tunes EMA length and guidance separately per metric: FID and FD_DINOv2 disagree strongly (EMA 2% vs 14% at guidance 1.4; best guidance 1.4 for FID vs 1.9 for FD_DINOv2).
entries.quote: their preferred EMA lengths are totally different (2% vs 14%). FID considers FD_DINOv2's optimum (14%) to be a terrible choice and vice versa. ... The significant differences in the optimal EMA length highlight the importance of searching the optimum specifically for the chosen quality metric. Third, FD_DINOv2 prefers higher guidance strength than FID (1.9 vs 1.4). FID considers 1.9 clearly excessive.
entries.source: Karras et al. 2024, Analyzing and Improving the Training Dynamics of Diffusion Models (EDM2)
entries.note: Also: 'FD_DINOv2 prefers images with better global coherency, which often maps to higher perceptual quality, corroborating the conclusions of Stein et al.'

entries.claim: The CMMD paper argues FID contradicts human raters, misses gradual improvement in iterative text-to-image models, misses distortions and is inconsistent across sample sizes.
entries.quote: We empirically demonstrate that FID contradicts human raters, it does not reflect gradual improvement of iterative text-to-image models, it does not capture distortion levels, and that it produces inconsistent results when varying the sample size.
entries.source: Jayasumana et al. 2024, Rethinking FID: Towards a Better Evaluation Metric for Image Generation (CVPR 2024)

entries.claim: CMMD is the squared MMD between CLIP ViT-L/14@336px embeddings of real and generated images with a Gaussian RBF kernel, sigma = 10, multiplied by 1000 for readability; the paper presents the unbiased (diagonal-excluded) estimator.
entries.quote: we use the Gaussian RBF kernel k(x,y)=exp(-||x-y||^2/2σ^2), which is a characteristic kernel, with the bandwidth parameter set to σ=10. ... Since the MMD metric with the Gaussian kernel is bounded above at 2 ..., it gives small values for general distributions. We therefore scale up the value in Eq. (4) by 1000 to obtain more readable values. For the CLIP embedding model, we use the publicly-available ViT-L/14@336px model
entries.source: Jayasumana et al. 2024, Rethinking FID: Towards a Better Evaluation Metric for Image Generation
entries.where: Section 4, Eq. (4) and paragraph after 'Some advantages of MMD'
entries.note: Eq. (4) in the paper is the unbiased U-statistic (sums over j != i, normalised by m(m-1)). The official code uses the biased V-statistic instead: see cmmd_code_distance.

entries.claim: Evaluating Stable Diffusion on random COCO-30K subsets, FID needs more than 20,000 images to stabilise while CMMD is consistent even with small sets.
entries.quote: Note that we need more than 20,000 images to reliably estimate FID, whereas CMMD provides consistent estimates even with small image sets.
entries.source: Jayasumana et al. 2024, Rethinking FID

entries.claim: On all 1,633 PartiPrompts, raters preferred the full Muse model over an early-stopped one 92.5% to 6.9%, yet COCO-30K FID and FID_infinity favoured the worse model; CMMD agreed with the raters.
entries.quote: Table 3: Model-A / Model-B: FID 21.40 / 18.42; FID_∞ 20.16 / 17.19; CMMD 0.721 / 0.951; Human rater preference 92.5% / 6.9%. 'FID contradicts human evaluation while CMMD agrees.' ... 'All image pairs were rated by 3 independent raters' ... 'The raters were indifferent 0.6% of the time.'
entries.source: Jayasumana et al. 2024, Rethinking FID

entries.claim: The CMMD paper describes KID as using a rational quadratic kernel, which disagrees with the KID paper's cubic polynomial kernel.
entries.quote: KID utilizes the squared MMD distance with the rational quadratic kernel.
entries.source: Jayasumana et al. 2024, Rethinking FID
entries.note: Disagreement: Binkowski et al. 2018 define KID with k(x,y) = (x.y/d + 1)^3 (see kid_definition) and torch-fidelity defaults to that poly kernel. Treat the CMMD paper's description as an error.

entries.claim: The official CMMD code sets _SIGMA = 10 and _SCALE = 1000 and computes the biased (minimum-variance) MMD with jnp.mean over full kernel matrices, so the diagonal terms k(x_i,x_i) = 1 are included, unlike the paper's unbiased Eq. (4).
entries.quote: _SIGMA = 10 ... _SCALE = 1000 ... This implements the minimum-variance/biased version of the estimator described in Eq.(5) of https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume13/gretton12a/gretton12a.pdf. As described in Lemma 6's proof in that paper, the unbiased estimate and the minimum-variance estimate for MMD are almost identical. ... k_xx = jnp.mean(jnp.exp(-gamma * (...))) ... return _SCALE * (k_xx + k_yy - 2 * k_xy)
entries.source: Google Research, CMMD official code (google-research/google-research, cmmd/distance.py)
entries.where: cmmd/distance.py lines 25 (_SIGMA), 28 (_SCALE), 35--39 (docstring), 58--90 (estimator); repo commit 3ef52111c1fabc301880818f5a547570e926a76b (last change to cmmd/ is 5b09c22d73a9d35eb6c5d2a99b95677a45053466)
entries.note: Paper vs code disagreement: paper Section 4 calls CMMD 'an unbiased estimator' and gives Eq. (4) with j != i; code uses the biased version. With m = n samples the biased estimate exceeds the unbiased one by roughly (2 - 2*mean off-diagonal kernel)/n scaled by 1000, which shrinks as n grows.

entries.claim: The CMMD code embeds images with the scenic CLIP model 'vit_l14_336px': each image is centre-cropped to a square and resized with PIL bicubic to 336, scaled to [0,1], resized again with jax bicubic and CLIP-normalised.
entries.quote: _CLIP_MODEL_NAME = 'vit_l14_336px' ... images = jax.image.resize(images, shape=target_shape, method='bicubic') ... images = clip.normalize_image(images)  [io_util.py: def _center_crop_and_resize(im, size): ... im = im.crop(box) ... return im.resize((size, size), resample=Image.BICUBIC)]
entries.source: Google Research, CMMD official code (cmmd/embedding.py, cmmd/io_util.py)
entries.where: embedding.py lines 23 (model name), 26--35 (_clip_preprocess), 41--59; io_util.py lines 38--46 (_center_crop_and_resize), 139 (/255.0); commit 3ef52111c1fabc301880818f5a547570e926a76b
entries.note: io_util.py URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google-research/google-research/3ef52111c1fabc301880818f5a547570e926a76b/cmmd/io_util.py. Centre crop applies when reshape_to > 0, which main.py sets to the model input size (io_util.py line 122).

entries.claim: CLIPScore is 2.5 times the cosine similarity between CLIP ViT-B/32 image and caption embeddings, clipped at zero; it needs no reference captions.
entries.quote: For an image with visual CLIP embedding v and a candidate caption with textual CLIP embedding c, we set w=2.5 and compute CLIP-S as: CLIP-S(c, v) = w * max(cos(c, v), 0) ... The model we use is the ViT-B/32 version.
entries.source: Hessel, Holtzman, Forbes, Le Bras, Choi 2021, CLIPScore: A Reference-free Evaluation Metric for Image Captioning (EMNLP 2021)
entries.note: Raw cosines 'generally observe values ranging from roughly zero to roughly .4'; w = 2.5 stretches this toward [0,1]. They prefix captions with 'A photo depicts'. Appendix B: the rescaling parameters 'only apply to CLIP ViT-B/32'. Many text-to-image papers instead report 100 * cos (e.g. GenEval's CLIPScore column ~27--37), so CLIPScore scales differ between papers.

entries.claim: For caption evaluation on Flickr8K-Expert, reference-free CLIP-S reaches Kendall tau_c 51.2 with human judgments, above reference-based CIDEr (43.9) and SPICE (44.9); RefCLIP-S reaches 53.0.
entries.quote: Table 1 (Flickr8K-Expert, tau_c): BLEU-4 30.8; CIDEr 43.9; SPICE 44.9; ViLBERTScore-F 50.1; CLIP-S (no refs) 51.2; RefCLIP-S 53.0
entries.source: Hessel et al. 2021, CLIPScore: A Reference-free Evaluation Metric for Image Captioning
entries.note: This is a captioning benchmark (judging captions for real images), not text-to-image generation.

entries.claim: GenEval scores six object-focused tasks (single object, two object, counting, colors, position, attribute binding) with a Mask2Former instance segmenter for presence, count and position, and CLIP ViT-L/14 zero-shot classification on masked crops for colour; each image is pass/fail and the overall score is the mean over tasks.
entries.quote: For object detection and instance segmentation, we choose the best instance segmentation model available from the MMDetection toolbox [5], a Mask2Former [7] trained on MS COCO. ... For the colors and attribute binding tasks, we use the CLIP ViT-L/14 model [31] to classify object color. ... This score is averaged across all images generated for each task to obtain task-specific scores, and then averaged across the six tasks to produce an overall score
entries.source: Ghosh, Hajishirzi, Schmidt 2023, GenEval: An Object-Focused Framework for Evaluating Text-to-Image Alignment (NeurIPS 2023 D&B)
entries.note: Mask2Former with Swin-S backbone (Appendix). 553 prompts, 4 images each. Counting uses a raised detector confidence threshold of 0.9.

entries.claim: GenEval overall scores: SD v1.5 0.43, SD v2.1 0.50, SD-XL 0.55, IF-XL 0.61; position and attribute binding stay low (best 0.15 and 0.35).
entries.quote: Table 2, Overall (single / two / counting / colors / position / attr. binding / overall): SDv1.5 0.97/0.38/0.35/0.76/0.04/0.06/0.43; SDv2.1 0.98/0.51/0.44/0.85/0.07/0.17/0.50; SD-XL 0.98/0.74/0.39/0.85/0.15/0.23/0.55; IF-XL 0.97/0.74/0.66/0.81/0.13/0.35/0.61; minDALL-E 0.23 overall; CLIP retrieval (real LAION images) 0.35 overall
entries.source: Ghosh et al. 2023, GenEval
entries.note: DALL-E 2 and DALL-E 3 are not evaluated in the GenEval paper (unconfirmed there; later papers report them). Caption: 'Overall scores vary by 0.01--0.02 across random seeds.'

entries.claim: GenEval agrees with human annotators on 83% of images versus 88% inter-annotator agreement, rising to 91% on images where annotators were unanimous.
entries.quote: Overall, GenEval attains 83% agreement with annotators about the correctness of generated images, compared to the interannotator agreement of 88%. This agreement rate is boosted to 91% on images that annotators unanimously agree on
entries.source: Ghosh et al. 2023, GenEval
entries.note: Threshold-tuned CLIPScore has slightly higher agreement on single object and colors, GenEval higher on the other four tasks.

entries.claim: TIFA turns a prompt into question-answer pairs with GPT-3 (filtered by UnifiedQA), then asks a VQA model the questions about the generated image; the score is VQA accuracy. TIFA v1.0 has 4K prompts and 25K questions in 12 categories.
entries.quote: Given a repository of text inputs, we automatically generate question-answer pairs for each text via a language model (here, GPT-3 [3]). A question-answering (QA) system (here, UnifiedQA [25]) is subsequently used to verify and filter these question-answer pairs. To evaluate a generated image, we use a visual-question-answering (VQA) system (here, mPLUG-large [31], BLIP-2 [32], etc.) to answer the questions given the generated image.
entries.source: Hu et al. 2023, TIFA: Accurate and Interpretable Text-to-Image Faithfulness Evaluation with Question Answering (ICCV 2023)

entries.claim: TIFA with mPLUG correlates with human 1--5 faithfulness ratings at Spearman 0.597 versus 0.332 for CLIPScore.
entries.quote: Table 2 (Spearman rho / Kendall tau, x100): CLIPScore 33.2 / 23.1; TIFA (VILT) 49.3 / 38.2; TIFA (OFA) 49.6 / 37.2; TIFA (mPLUG) 59.7 / 47.2. Text: 'TIFA has much higher correlation with human judgments than CLIPScore (Spearman's rho = 0.60 vs. 0.33)'
entries.source: Hu et al. 2023, TIFA

entries.claim: VQAScore is the VQA model's probability of answering 'Yes' to 'Does this figure show "{text}"? Please answer yes or no.'; the authors' best model is CLIP-FlanT5 (bidirectional encoder-decoder), and they also report it with LLaVA-1.5 and InstructBLIP.
entries.quote: P("Yes" | image, "Does this figure show '{text}'? Please answer yes or no.") ... We term this approach VQAScore. Despite its simplicity, VQAScore implemented via open-source VQA models [47, 11] outperforms nearly all prior art including CLIPScore [21], models trained with extensive human feedback [87, 86, 33], and divide-and-conquer methods
entries.source: Lin et al. 2024, Evaluating Text-to-Visual Generation with Image-to-Text Generation (VQAScore, ECCV 2024)
entries.note: Motivation: CLIP text encoders 'can notoriously act as a "bag of words"'. Also introduces GenAI-Bench, 1,600 compositional prompts with over 15,000 human ratings.

entries.claim: On Winoground, VQAScore with CLIP-FlanT5 scores text/image/group 60.0/57.5/46.0 versus CLIPScore (CLIP-L-14) 27.8/11.5/7.8, PickScore 23.8/12.5/6.8 and HPSv2 11.5/7.8/4.0 (random 25/25/16.7).
entries.quote: Table 1 (Winoground text/image/group; EqBen text/image/group): Random Chance 25.0/25.0/16.7; CLIPScore (CLIP-L-14) 27.8/11.5/7.8, 35.0/35.0/25.0; PickScore 23.8/12.5/6.8; ImageReward 42.8/15.3/12.8; HPSv2 11.5/7.8/4.0; VQAScore LLaVA-1.5 45.5/41.3/29.8; VQAScore CLIP-FlanT5 60.0/57.5/46.0, 59.3/63.6/47.9; Human 89.5/88.5/85.5
entries.source: Lin et al. 2024, Evaluating Text-to-Visual Generation with Image-to-Text Generation (VQAScore)
entries.note: Text: 'Compared to baselines (e.g., CLIPScore [21] and PickScore [33]) that perform at chance-level, our VQAScore achieves 2x to 5x higher scores.'

entries.claim: Davidsonian Scene Graph generates atomic, unique questions arranged in a dependency graph so that a question like 'is the motorcycle blue?' is skipped when 'is there a motorcycle?' is answered no, fixing inconsistent VQA answers in TIFA-style QG/A; DSG-1k has 1,060 prompts.
entries.quote: if the answer to "is there a motorcycle?" is no, dependent questions like "is the motorcycle blue?" should be skipped – VQA models may often say "motorcycle doesn't exist but it's blue" ... DSG produces atomic and unique questions organized in dependency graphs, which (i) ensure appropriate semantic coverage and (ii) sidestep inconsistent answers.
entries.source: Cho et al. 2024, Davidsonian Scene Graph: Improving Reliability in Fine-grained Evaluation for Text-to-Image Generation (ICLR 2024)

entries.claim: T2I-CompBench (NeurIPS 2023) has 6,000 compositional prompts in attribute binding, object relationships and complex compositions, scored with disentangled BLIP-VQA (attributes), UniDet (spatial) and others; the current arXiv version is T2I-CompBench++ with 8,000 prompts and a numeracy category.
entries.quote: v1 abstract: 'T2I-CompBench, a comprehensive benchmark for open-world compositional text-to-image generation, consisting of 6,000 compositional text prompts from 3 categories (attribute binding, object relationships, and complex compositions) and 6 sub-categories'. Current HTML: 'T2I-CompBench++ comprises 8,000 compositional text prompts categorized into four primary groups: attribute binding, object relationships, generative numeracy, and complex compositions.'
entries.source: Huang, Sun, Xie, Li, Liu 2023, T2I-CompBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Open-world Compositional Text-to-image Generation (later T2I-CompBench++)
entries.where: v1 abstract; current version abstract at https://arxiv.org/html/2307.06350
entries.note: Version difference: cite 6,000 for the NeurIPS 2023 paper and 8,000 for T2I-CompBench++.

entries.claim: Pick-a-Pic collects real users' pairwise preferences from a web app: over 500,000 examples and 35,000 distinct prompts (583,747 training examples in the paper's snapshot), later released at over one million examples.
entries.quote: Overall, the Pick-a-Pic dataset contains over 500,000 examples and 35,000 distinct prompts. ... the reported experiments in this paper involve an NSFW filtered and not fully updated version of Pick-a-Pic, that contains 583,747 training examples, and 500 validation and test examples. ... We recently open-sourced a new version of the Pick-a-Pic dataset that has more than one million examples.
entries.source: Kirstain et al. 2023, Pick-a-Pic: An Open Dataset of User Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation (NeurIPS 2023)

entries.claim: PickScore, a fine-tuned CLIP-H, predicts held-out user preferences with 70.5% accuracy versus 68.0% for expert human annotators, 60.8% for zero-shot CLIP-H and 56.8% for the LAION aesthetics predictor (random 56.8% under the tie-aware metric).
entries.quote: Table 1(b), Pick-a-Pic test accuracy: Random 56.8; Human Expert 68.0; Aesthetics 56.8; CLIP-H 60.8; ImageReward 61.1; HPS 66.7; PickScore (Ours) 70.5
entries.source: Kirstain et al. 2023, Pick-a-Pic: An Open Dataset of User Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation
entries.note: Backbone: CLIP-H fine-tuned with an InstructGPT-style reward objective. Accuracy is 'an adapted accuracy metric that accounts for the possibility of a tie', so random is 56.8 not 50. The 'human experts' are 'friends and colleagues of the authors' who lack the prompter's context. Text refers to this as 'Table 4(b)', a labelling slip; values match.

entries.claim: Model-level Elo ratings computed from PickScore correlate 0.790 with real users' Elo ratings, versus 0.670 for HPS, 0.492 for ImageReward and 0.313 for CLIP-H.
entries.quote: PickScore exhibits a stronger correlation (0.790±0.054) with real users than all other automatic metrics, namely CLIP-H (0.313±0.075), ImageReward (0.492±0.086), and HPS (0.670±0.071).
entries.source: Kirstain et al. 2023, Pick-a-Pic

entries.claim: HPD v2 holds 798,090 human preference choices; the training split is 107,515 groups of 4 images ranked by one annotator (645,090 binary comparisons), and the test set is annotated by 10 annotators each (153,000 comparisons).
entries.quote: HPD v2 comprises 798,090 human preference choices on 433,760 pairs of images, making it the largest dataset of its kind. ... The training split of HPD v2 contains 107,515 groups of images, each containing 4 images from 4 models (or real image), ranked by one annotator, which corresponds to 645,090 human binary comparisons. ... Each group in the test set is annotated by 10 distinct annotators ... resulting in 153,000 binary comparisons.
entries.source: Wu et al. 2023, Human Preference Score v2: A Solid Benchmark for Evaluating Human Preferences of Text-to-Image Synthesis
entries.note: Internal wording disagreement: the abstract says '433,760 pairs of images', Section 3 says '798k pairs of binary preference choices for 434k images'. The 434k figure appears to be an image count. 645,090 + 153,000 = 798,090, consistent.

entries.claim: HPS v2 (OpenCLIP ViT-H/14 fine-tuned) reaches 83.3% on the HPD v2 test set and 65.7% on the ImageReward test set, above PickScore (79.8 / 62.9), ImageReward (74.0 / 65.1), aesthetics (76.8 / 57.4) and zero-shot CLIP ViT-H/14 (65.1 / 57.1).
entries.quote: Table 6 (ImageReward test / HPD v2 test): CLIP ViT-H/14 57.1 / 65.1; ImageReward 65.1 / 74.0; Aesthetic Score Predictor 57.4 / 76.8; HPS 61.2 / 77.6; PickScore 62.9 / 79.8; Single Human vs. Single Human 65.3 / 78.1; Single Human vs. Averaged Human 53.9 / 85.0; HPS v2 65.7 / 83.3
entries.source: Wu et al. 2023, Human Preference Score v2
entries.note: Backbone: 'We fine-tune ViT-H/14 trained by OpenCLIP' (LAION-2B), 4,000 steps.

entries.claim: ImageReward is trained on expert annotations of 8,878 prompts giving 136,892 pairwise comparisons (the '137k'), with a BLIP backbone (ViT-L image encoder) because BLIP beat CLIP in their ablation.
entries.quote: After 2 months of annotation, we collected valid annotations for 8,878 prompts, resulting in 136,892 compared pairs. ... We use BLIP [26] as the backbone of ImageReward, as it outperforms conventional CLIP (Cf. Table 2(b)) in our preliminary experiments.
entries.source: Xu et al. 2023, ImageReward: Learning and Evaluating Human Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation (NeurIPS 2023)

entries.claim: On the 466-prompt test set (6,399 comparisons) ImageReward predicts preferences with 65.14% accuracy versus 54.82% for CLIP score, 57.35% for the aesthetic score and 57.76% for BLIP score.
entries.quote: Table 3, Preference Acc.: CLIP Score 54.82; Aesthetic Score 57.35; BLIP Score 57.76; ImageReward (Ours) 65.14. Text: 'The preference accuracy of ImageReward reaches up to 65.14%, which is 15.14% more than 50% (random), about twice as much as 7.76% (that of BLIP score).'
entries.source: Xu et al. 2023, ImageReward
entries.note: The introduction claims ImageReward 'outperforms ... CLIP (by 38.6%), Aesthetic (by 39.6%), and BLIP (by 31.6%)'; these percentages do not follow directly from the Table 3 accuracies (gap is 10.3, 7.8, 7.4 points), so they are some other relative measure; cite the table values instead.

entries.quote: textToImage list: "GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst (max)","elo":1219.65,"lower95ci":1209.65,"upper95ci":1229.65; "GPT Image 2.5 Flare (max)","elo":1207.2 (1197.2--1217.2); "GPT Image 2 (high)","elo":1185.56 (1173.56--1197.56); "Nano Banana 2.1","elo":1174.33 (1162.33--1186.33); "Grok Imagine Image 2.0","elo":1166.81 (1153.81--1179.81); "FLUX.2 [dev]","elo":1000,"lower95ci":1000,"upper95ci":1000. Page text: 'Elo scores from blind preference votes by our validated private evaluators.'
entries.source: Artificial Analysis, Image Arena / Compare Models (text to image)

A per-model chart on the same page shows slightly different values for some models (e.g. Nano Banana 2.1 absent there; MAI-Image-2.5 1116.37), so ranks below the top three depend on which view is used. FLUX.2 [dev] fixed at 1000 with zero-width CI suggests it is the Elo anchor (inferred, not stated).

Oct 7, 2026 6,604,125 votes 82 models ... 1 | gpt-image-2.5-sunburst OpenAI · Proprietary | 1425±7 Preliminary | 17,752; 2 | gpt-image-2.5-flare | 1398±7 Preliminary | 16,889; 3 | gpt-image-2 (medium) | 1383±4 | 93,334; 4 | grok-imagine-image-2.0 (canvas) SpaceXAI | 1334±12 Preliminary | 3,113; 5 | mai-image-2.6 Microsoft AI | 1332±5 | 25,091; 6 | gemini-nano-banana-2.1 | 1328±9 Preliminary | 5,310

Rank spreads: ranks 4--6 share spread 4--6, i.e. statistically tied. Scores are on a different scale from Artificial Analysis Elo, so compare ranks, not numbers.

entries.claim: POPE measures object hallucination by asking 'Is there a <object> in the image?' for real objects and for absent objects chosen at random, from the most frequent dataset objects (popular), or from objects that most co-occur with those present (adversarial); it reports accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and the yes-ratio.
entries.quote: Random Sampling: we randomly sample the objects that do not exist in the image. Popular Sampling: we select the top-k most frequent objects in the whole image dastaset that do not exist in the current image, where k=l/2. Adversarial Sampling: we first rank all objects according to their co-occurring frequencies with the ground-truth objects, and then select the top-k frequent ones that do not exist in the image. ... We adopt Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1 score as the evaluation metrics. ... Besides, we also report the ratio that LVLMs answer "Yes" as a reference
entries.source: Li et al. 2023, Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (POPE, EMNLP 2023)
entries.note: MSCOCO val: 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects, 6 questions each (half yes, half no). F1 is the 'major metric'.

entries.claim: On POPE (MSCOCO), the original LLaVA answers 'yes' about 95--99% of the time, so its accuracy is near 50%, while InstructBLIP reaches F1 89.29 (random), 83.45 (popular) and 78.45 (adversarial).
entries.source: Li et al. 2023, Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (POPE)
entries.note: LLaVA here is the original 2023 LLaVA, not LLaVA-1.5. A yes-always model gets F1 66.67 (MultiModal-GPT row: 50.00 / 50.00 / 100.00 / 66.67 / 100.00), which is why the yes-ratio matters.

entries.claim: MMBench's CircularEval asks each N-choice question N times with the options circularly shifted and counts it correct only if every pass is right; this drops accuracy for most models, e.g. OpenFlamingo v2 from 36.7% to 2.6% and GPT-4v by 10.8 points.
entries.quote: each question is fed to a VLM N times (N is the number of choices). Each time, circular shifting is applied to the choices and the answer to generate a new prompt for VLMs ... A VLM is considered successful in solving a question only if it correctly predicts the answer in all circular passes. ... the performance of OpenFlamingo v2 drops from 36.7% to only 2.6% when we move from VanillaEval to CircularEval. Table 2: GPT-4v 74.3% (-10.8%); LLaVA-v1.5-7B 62.5% (-11.2%); InstructBLIP-7B 37.4% (-24.0%); OpenFlamingo v2 2.6% (-34.1%)
entries.source: Liu et al. 2024, MMBench: Is Your Multi-modal Model an All-around Player? (ECCV 2024)
entries.note: Motivation: 'random guessing will lead to ~25% Top-1 accuracy for 4-choice questions' and models favour certain option letters.

entries.claim: OCRBench has 1,000 question-answer pairs in five components: text recognition, scene-text VQA, document VQA, key information extraction and handwritten mathematical expression recognition; the full study spans 29 datasets.
entries.quote: OCRBench consists of five components: text recognition, Scene Text-Centric VQA, Document-Oriented VQA, KIE, and HMER. It includes 1000 question-answer pairs
entries.source: Liu et al. 2024, OCRBench: On the Hidden Mystery of OCR in Large Multimodal Models
entries.where: Section on OCRBench; Appendix Table 5 (composition: text recognition 300, scene-text VQA 200, doc VQA 200, ...)

entries.claim: Many VLM benchmark questions can be answered without the image: GeminiPro scores 42.9% on MMMU with no visual input (random 22.1%), and Sphinx-X-MoE gets 43.6% on MMMU without images; MMStar keeps 1,500 human-checked vision-indispensable samples.
entries.quote: For instance, GeminiPro achieves 42.9% on the MMMU benchmark without any visual input, and outperforms the random choice baseline across six benchmarks over 24% on average. ... Sphinx-X-MoE gets 43.6% on MMMU without accessing images, surpassing its LLM backbone with 17.9%. ... MMStar, an elite vision-indispensable multi-modal benchmark comprising 1,500 samples meticulously selected by humans. MMStar benchmarks 6 core capabilities and 18 detailed axes
entries.source: Chen et al. 2024, Are We on the Right Way for Evaluating Large Vision-Language Models? (MMStar, NeurIPS 2024)
entries.where: Abstract; Table 1 (0-shot LLMs): GeminiPro MMMU 42.9, Avg 41.4; Random Choice MMMU 22.1, Avg 18.7
entries.note: Small text vs table gap: '24% on average' over random; Table 1 gives 41.4 - 18.7 = 22.7 points (0-shot) and Table 2 gives 42.4 - 18.7 = 23.7 (2-shot). Also: 'more than 50% questions of ScienceQA and 20% questions of MMMU can be solved by most LLMs directly.'

entries.claim: FVD applies the Frechet distance to features of an I3D action-recognition network trained on Kinetics; the authors chose the logits layer of the Kinetics-400 I3D.
entries.quote: we investigate several variations of a pre-trained Inflated 3D Convnet (I3D; [5]), and name the resulting metric the Fréchet Video Distance (FVD). The I3D network generalizes the Inception architecture to sequential data, and is trained to perform action-recognition on the Kinetics data set ... it can be seen that the logits layer of the I3D model pre-trained on Kinetics-400 is among the best performing configurations
entries.source: Unterthiner et al. 2018, Towards Accurate Generative Models of Video: A New Metric & Challenges
entries.note: The same paper defines a Kernel Video Distance (KVD) with the KID polynomial kernel on I3D features.

entries.claim: FVD is biased toward per-frame image quality over motion: heavy temporal corruption raises it only slightly, and cherry-picking motionless generated videos can lower it a lot; features from self-supervised video models (e.g. VideoMAE-v2) are less biased.
entries.quote: We first quantify the FVD's sensitivity to the temporal axis by decoupling the frame and motion quality and find that the FVD increases only slightly with large temporal corruption. We then analyze the generated videos and show that via careful sampling from a large set of generated videos that do not contain motions, one can drastically decrease FVD without improving the temporal quality. ... We show that FVD with features extracted from the recent large-scale self-supervised video models is less biased toward image quality.
entries.source: Ge et al. 2024, On the Content Bias in Frechet Video Distance (CVPR 2024)
entries.note: The specific self-supervised model (VideoMAE-v2) is named in the paper body; only the abstract was quoted here.

entries.claim: FAD computes the Frechet distance between Gaussians fitted to VGGish embeddings of evaluated audio and of a large background set of studio music; on artificial distortions it correlated 0.52 with human ratings versus 0.39 for SDR.
entries.quote: Where FID uses the activations from a hidden layer in the Inception network [18] to generate embeddings, FAD uses embeddings generated by the VGGish [6] model. ... We show that, with a correlation coefficient of 0.52, FAD correlates more closely with human perception than either SDR, cosine distance or magnitude L2 distance, with correlation coefficients of 0.39, -0.15 and -0.01 respectively.
entries.source: Kilgour, Zuluaga, Roblek, Sharifi 2018, Frechet Audio Distance: A Metric for Evaluating Music Enhancement Algorithms
entries.where: Abstract; Section 3; Section 4 (Figure 7, Plackett-Luce worth values)
entries.note: Human ratings were pairwise comparisons turned into Plackett-Luce worth values per distortion; 'correlation coefficient' as stated (type not specified in the quoted text). FAD was introduced for music enhancement, not generation. VGGish input: 96 frames of 64-d log-mel over 1 s windows.

entries.claim: VBench splits video generation quality into 16 disentangled dimensions (e.g. subject consistency, motion smoothness), each with its own prompts and evaluator, validated against human preference annotations.
entries.quote: VBench comprises 16 dimensions in video generation (e.g., subject identity inconsistency, motion smoothness, tempor[al flickering ...])
entries.source: Huang et al. 2024, VBench: Comprehensive Benchmark Suite for Video Generative Models (CVPR 2024)

entries.claim: ADM (guided diffusion) uses the entire training set as the FID reference batch, recomputes all baselines with one codebase, and uses 10k instead of 50k samples only for its ablation plots.
entries.quote: To ensure consistent comparisons, we use the entire training set as the reference batch Heusel et al. (2017); Brock et al. (2018), and evaluate metrics for all models using the same codebase. ... [Figure 2 caption] FID evaluated over 10k samples instead of 50k for efficiency.
entries.source: Dhariwal and Nichol 2021, Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis
entries.note: The paper also cites 'subtle implementation differences can affect the resulting FID values Parmar et al. (2021)' as a reason to recompute baselines. The 50k default is stated explicitly in the code README (adm_eval_readme), only implicitly in the paper.

entries.claim: The guided-diffusion evaluation suite ships reference batches with statistics over the whole dataset plus 10,000 images for precision/recall, and sample batches of 50,000 images; it reports FID, sFID, precision, recall and IS.
entries.quote: To compare different generative models, we use FID, sFID, Precision, Recall, and Inception Score. ... Reference dataset batches contain pre-computed statistics over the whole dataset, as well as 10,000 images for computing Precision and Recall. All other batches contain 50,000 images which can be used to compute statistics and Precision/Recall.
entries.source: OpenAI guided-diffusion repository, evaluations/README.md

entries.claim: The common convention is 50,000 generated images against statistics of the full training set: Heusel et al. generate 50,000; EDM2 uses 50,000 generated vs all 1,281,167 ImageNet images 'following the established best practices in FID computation'; ADM uses the entire training set as reference.
entries.quote: Heusel: 'we generate 50,000 images'; EDM2: 'We use 50,000 generated images and all 1,281,167 available real images, following the established best practices in FID computation.'; ADM: 'we use the entire training set as the reference batch'
entries.source: Heusel et al. 2017; Karras et al. 2024 (EDM2); Dhariwal and Nichol 2021
entries.note: Cross-reference entry built from the three sources listed (URLs in those entries). StyleGAN2 paper was not fetched, so its protocol is unconfirmed here. Chong and Forsyth note some papers use FID_10k instead.
